p.title: Should Moving to the Middle Win Candidates Votes? It Depends Where Voters Are

ext.title: Should Moving to the Middle Win Candidates Votes? It Depends Where Voters Are
ext.venue: Not stated in the text. The metadata hint says OSF Preprints; the PDF text does not name a venue, so this is unconfirmed.
ext.doi: Not in the text. The hint's 10.31235/osf.io/bvjtd_v1 could not be confirmed from the PDF. The paper cites a pre-registration at https://osf.io/qpgsf (footnote 13), which is a different OSF object.
ext.document_type: Working paper / manuscript (dated March 11, 2026; "Associate Professor" affiliations at UC Berkeley and Yale; no journal named)
ext.coverage: Read all 3,836 lines of the text file (main text pp. 1-24, references pp. 24-28, Online Appendix A-H pp. A1-A35, including Tables A1-A10 and the full policy-position text). Annotations: one file, _annots/5892b625ebfc.json, containing 40 Highlight items, all by Paul Goff. None has note text (the content field is empty for all 40) and there are no sticky notes or text boxes. Lobbying, network analysis, path-finding and resource allocation do not appear as methods. Election-related content covers candidate positioning, vote choice and persuasion. The paper cites donor and endorsement work only in passing. Correction to the metadata hint: the year is 2026 per the text date, and the venue and DOI could not be verified from the text.
ext.research_question: Why do candidates appear to gain only modestly from moving toward the other party's positions, and does that small measured effect mean voters do not vote on issues? The paper asks whether relaxing two common assumptions (that movement toward the other party or the elite middle is movement toward the median voter, and that voter preferences are one-dimensional) can make the measured effect small even when every voter votes on issues.
ext.theory: Spatial model of elections (Black 1948; Downs 1957). Two assumptions are relaxed: (1) movement toward the other party or the "elite middle" equals movement toward the median voter, and (2) voters' preferences are one-dimensional. With multidimensional, cross-pressured voters and party positions that can be popular, moving toward the elite middle can win some voters and lose others. The net effect can be null or negative even when all voters vote on issues (Figure 1c, pp. 7-9). The argument is partial equilibrium and does not model candidate entry or general-equilibrium position choice.
ext.data: Survey conjoint experiment fielded by Verasight on 6,000 registered voters matched to the L2 voter file who voted in the 2024 general election and gave informed consent. Weighted with Verasight weights to the 2024 general electorate (Table A1, which also lists demographics). Unit of analysis: respondent x task x candidate x policy (N(Dem) = 180,000 and N(Rep) = 180,000 observations in regression tables; 6,000 respondents x 10 tasks x 3 policies). Each respondent completed a pre-treatment battery on 5 randomly selected of 29 policy issues. Pilot: 4,028 Prolific respondents, August 2025 (Appendix F). Fielding dates of the main study are not stated in the text. Candidates: 2028 hypothetical pairs of real politicians (Table A2 lists 26 names with perceived ideology and name recognition; Table A3 candidate-level vote shares).
ext.method: Forced-choice conjoint with two candidates (one Democrat, one Republican) per task, each with three randomly assigned issue positions from a bank of 29. Each position is independently assigned to the standard party position or the elite middle position with equal probability. Primary estimand: AMCE of adopting the elite middle position. Estimating equation (Eq. 1, p. 12): Y_ijk = alpha + beta * EliteMiddle_ijk + X_i gamma + e_ijk, estimated separately for Democratic and Republican candidates, with pre-registered pre-treatment covariates (ideology, presidential vote, share liberal in district/state, race, college, party ID 1-7 in Tables A4-A9). Heterogeneity: interactions with policy-domain indicators, terciles of public support for the liberal position (Figure 4), and an indicator for majority support for the party's standard position (Figure 5). Individual-level analyses split by the respondent's own pre-measured issue position (Figures 6-7). Standard errors clustered by respondent; survey weights applied throughout. Pre-registered at OSF (footnote 13). The estimator is described only as a linear model of the form in Eq. 1; the paper does not name it explicitly.
ext.identification: Randomized conjoint design. Each candidate's position on each issue is independently randomized between the standard party position and the elite middle position, so the elite-middle coefficient is identified by randomization within the experiment (AMCE). Candidate names are real and the perceived-party positions were validated (Figure A1: large majorities identified party positions). The estimand is partial-equilibrium and does not capture candidate entry, general-equilibrium repositioning or campaign-level persuasion.
ext.scope: Population: US registered voters who voted in the 2024 general election (weighted to the 2024 electorate). Institution: hypothetical 2028 presidential general-election matchups in a survey experiment, not actual elections. Era: current public opinion as of fielding (after 2024); the paper states its findings describe incentives under current opinion. Issues: 29 domains (abortion, immigration, healthcare, taxes, etc.) that map onto party divides; emerging non-partisan issues were dropped after the pilot.

key_findings.finding: Average effect of adopting the elite middle position (vs standard party position) on one of three issues: Democratic candidates gain 1.1 pp, Republican candidates gain 1.8 pp, both p < 0.001. Described as modest.

Issue heterogeneity is substantial. Democratic effects range from about -1.7 pp (Social Security) to +4.5 pp (affirmative action). Republican effects range from -4.2 pp (transgender sports) to +7.3 pp (gays and lesbians).
key_findings.numbers: Dem: -1.7 to +4.5 pp; Rep: -4.2 to +7.3 pp

key_findings.finding: Returns are largest where the party's standard position is least popular. Democrats benefit most on policies where their standard position is furthest from the median voter (more conservative public). Republicans benefit most where the public is liberal. Little benefit where the party already reflects majority sentiment.
key_findings.numbers: Dem tercile-1 interaction +0.0215 (SE 0.0028), tercile-2 +0.0105 (SE 0.0031), tercile-3 -0.0001 (SE 0.0032); Rep tercile-1 +0.0008 (SE 0.0029), tercile-2 +0.0229 (SE 0.0030), tercile-3 +0.0319 (SE 0.0032). Tercile labels as printed in Table A6.

key_findings.finding: On issues where a majority prefers the party's standard position, moving to the elite middle has a null or negative effect. The Republican effect is significant (about -2.4 pp, p < 0.001). The Democratic effect is negative and not significant.
key_findings.numbers: Rep majority-issue -0.0237 (SE 0.0048); Dem majority-issue -0.0042 (SE 0.0041); Rep non-majority +0.0247 (SE 0.0020); Dem non-majority +0.0142 (SE 0.0019)

key_findings.finding: At the individual level, the same move helps and hurts the same candidate. Respondents who hold the party's standard position on an issue do not reward the elite-middle move and may penalize it. Republican candidates lose among respondents who hold the Republican position (about -3.6 pp). Democratic respondents with the Democratic position show a non-significant effect.

Respondents classified as overall moderate (mixed positions across issues) still reward moving to the elite middle only on issues where they disagree with the party's standard position. Moderates who agree with the Republican position on an issue penalize Republican candidates who move to the elite middle.
key_findings.location: pp. 20-21; Figure 7; Table A9 (Table A9 covers the moderate subsample)
key_findings.numbers: Rep candidate, own=R -0.0524 (SE 0.0112); Rep candidate, own=D +0.0381 (SE 0.0072); Dem candidate, own=D -0.0011 (SE 0.0113), own=R +0.0239 (SE 0.0069). Per Table A9's note, the moderate subsample is N(Dem) = 5,056-7,983 and N(Rep) = 4,806-10,404 across columns.

key_findings.finding: Less than 10% of respondents gave consistently Democratic, Republican, or elite-middle answers across all five issues. The authors read this as cross-pressure, not measurement error.
The paper's main claim is interpretive. A small average return to moderation does not show voters ignore issues. Voters vote on issues, but in a multidimensional way that one-dimensional models miss.
key_findings.location: Introduction p. 2-4; Figure 1c p. 8; Conclusion pp. 21-24

key_findings.finding: Results are reported as roughly linear in the number of elite-middle positions a candidate takes, with limited interaction between the two candidates' choices.
key_findings.location: Appendix Figure A10 (text reference on p. 14, footnote 15)

key_findings.finding: Pilot (4,028 Prolific respondents, Aug 2025): adding candidate messages had minimal effects. Emerging non-partisan issues (school phones, monopoly policy, supply constraints) gave no consistent evidence of vote-share effects; some evidence on supply-constraint items.
Figure 1c is a stylized two-dimension example, not an empirical estimate. Figure A7 describes a stylized case in which 50% more voters respond to positioning than the net-effect calculation shows.
key_findings.numbers: Figure A7 illustration: 50% more responsive voters than the net estimate

measures: Outcome: binary forced choice of the Democratic or Republican candidate in each conjoint task (coded as chose own-party candidate in Tables A7-A9).
Treatment: ElitMiddle indicator, 1 if the candidate took the elite-middle position on an issue rather than the standard party position.
Issue-level public support for liberal position (0-1), used for Figure A3 and tercile analysis (Figure 4).
Majority-support indicator: issue where more than 50% of respondents prefer the party's standard position (Figure 5).
Respondent own position on each pre-measured issue (liberal, moderate/elite middle, conservative), from five randomly selected issues per respondent.
Overall moderate respondent: holds liberal positions on fewer than 75% of issues (Democratic analysis) or more than 25% (Republican analysis) (p. 19).

Perceived candidate ideology (0 = very liberal, 1 = very conservative) and don't-know rate (Table A2). Perceived extremism is the absolute deviation from 0.5 (Figure A6). Vote margin per candidate (Table A3).
limitations: Conjoint presents candidates in a stylized format without established records, less-informed voters, or turnout dynamics (p. 23; Hall and Thompson 2018).
The 29 issues do not exhaust the policy space, and different elite-middle positions could yield different results (p. 23).
Partial equilibrium only. Nationalized elections could also contribute to modest returns to moderation (p. 24; Colao et al. forthcoming).
Findings describe electoral incentives under current public opinion. Persuasion can shift opinion on transgender and undocumented-immigrant policies, which could change calculations (p. 24).
Partisan cue-taking and thermostatic backlash suggest that simply adopting a position is unlikely to move opinion toward it, and could move it the other way (p. 24).
Standard party positions were assumed to be perceived as party positions. Validation (Figure A1) shows large majorities identified them, but not for all issues in every subgroup.
Candidate-level results (Appendix E) are exploratory. The same positions were signaled for all same-party candidates, which may understate moderate candidates' advantages (p. A13-A14).
Hypothetical survey effects are not interpreted as precise magnitudes ('we do not ascribe much importance to the point estimates').
Alternative interpretation (footnote 14): the mixed responses could reflect one-dimensional preferences with different issue cutlines for voters and elites.

Future research directions: why parties take unpopular positions (Figures A11-A12 suggest primary voters are not entirely responsible), whether returns change as opinion evolves, and field experiments with real campaign communications (p. 24).

references_of_note: Bawn, Cohen, Karol, Masket, Noel and Zaller 2012, 'A Theory of Political Parties: Groups, Policy Demands and Nominations in American Politics', Perspectives on Politics 10(3). Party-groups theory cited as one source of the skeptical reading.

Broockman and Malhotra 2020, 'What do partisan donors want?', Public Opinion Quarterly 84(1). Donors pull parties apart (Democrats left on social issues, Republicans right on economic issues), which the paper links to the out-of-step pattern (p. 17).

Colao, Broockman, Huber and Kalla, forthcoming, 'Issues, Endorsements, And Vote Choice: A Panel Study Of Congressional Primary And General Elections', AJPS. Endorsements and primary elections as a nationalized-election alternative (p. 24).
Bonica, Rhee and Studen 2025, 'The Electoral Consequences of Ideological Persuasion', SSRN. Within-precinct moderation estimate that the paper says is modest (p. 1).

Ansolabehere, Snyder and Stewart 2001, 'Candidate Positioning in U.S. House Elections', AJPS 45(1). Two-SD positioning shift gives about 3 points; the district midpoint measure is the one the paper critiques (p. 1, footnotes 1 and 3).
Canes-Wrone, Brady and Cogan 2002, 'The Electoral Behavior of Moderate Candidates', APSR 96(4). Uses ADA scores; 1-3 points per SD (footnotes 1 and 3).
Hall 2015, 'What happens when extremists win primaries?', APSR 109(1). Larger but noisily estimated moderation effect (footnote 1).
Hall and Thompson 2018, 'Who punishes extremist nominees?', APSR 112(3). Turnout dynamics cited as a limitation (p. 23).
Bafumi and Herron 2010, 'Leapfrog representation and extremism', APSR 104(3). Voters near the elite middle; the central contrasting claim.
Fowler, Hill, Lewis, Tausanovitch, Vavreck and Warshaw 2023, 'Moderates', APSR 117(2). One-dimensional account of mass ideology.
Achen and Bartels 2016, Democracy for Realists. Argument that voters do not vote on issues, which the paper contests.
Nyhan, McGhee, Sides, Masket and Greene 2012, 'One vote out of step?', American Politics Research 40(5). Out-of-step issue votes can move vote shares (p. 10, p. 23).
Broockman 2016, 'Approaches to studying policy representation', Legislative Studies Quarterly 41(1). Cross-pressured voters and multidimensional preferences.
Hainmueller, Hopkins and Yamamoto 2014 (conjoint causal inference) and Bansak et al. 2023 (AMCE in election outcomes). Methodological basis of the design.
Hinich 1977, 'Equilibrium in spatial voting: The median voter result is an artifact', JET 16(2). Vote-maximizing position is the median (or mean) voter (p. 8).
Enelow and Hinich 1984, The Spatial Theory of Voting. General-equilibrium extensions the paper sets aside (p. 5).

short_quotes.quote: Small measured effects of moderation may understate how many voters vote on issues.

rel.summary_md:
Broockman and Kalla run a pre-registered forced-choice conjoint with 6,000 verified 2024 voters (Verasight, weighted). Respondents choose between hypothetical 2028 presidential pairs of real politicians. On each of three issues, drawn from a bank of 29, each candidate is randomly given either the party's standard position or an "elite middle" position. Pooled, the move to the middle gains Democrats +1.1 pp and Republicans +1.8 pp. The authors argue that this pooled figure hides offsetting effects, so it should only be quoted with its strata. The effect is largest where the party's own position is unpopular (Republicans +3.2 pp in the most liberal-opinion tercile). Where a majority already backs the party's position, the effect is null or negative (Republicans -2.4 pp). At the individual level, voters who hold the party's position punish the move (Republican-position holders -3.6 pp), while voters who disagree reward it. Even "moderate" respondents reward the move only on issues where they disagree with the party, and fewer than 10% answered consistently across five issues. The authors' reading is that voters do vote on issues, but along several dimensions at once, so gains and losses cancel out in the average.

For Paul's systems, the paper bears mainly on Terrier's canvass layer. Terrier's support score and its "undecided" persuasion term both treat a person's partisan midpoint as the place where persuadability lives. That is a one-dimensional reading. The paper suggests that a mixed partisan score usually marks a cross-pressured voter: someone who can be moved on particular issues and pushed away on others, not a voter persuadable in general. Terrier has no data on voters' issue positions and no input for the candidate's positions, so it cannot represent this. For Melange, the evidence carries over only by analogy, because the paper studies voters, not legislators. Its main structural lesson for Melange is that an average across issues hides offsetting issue-level responses. Any use of this paper in the system stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Voters who are moderate on average reward a candidate's move to the elite middle only on issues where they disagree with the party. Among moderates holding the Republican position, the Republican-candidate effect is -0.0524 (SE 0.0112), against +0.0381 among moderates holding the Democratic position. Fewer than 10% of respondents gave consistent answers across five issues. Persuadability is therefore issue-specific and two-signed, not a property of sitting at the partisan midpoint.
bearings.system_side: The code computes undecided = (1 - |2s - 1|) x t, which peaks at s = 0.5. Here s is a composite of partisan, presidential, registration and primary-ballot lean, and the persuasion weight wp defaults to 0.5. Persuadability is assumed to be highest at the partisan midpoint among likely voters. The term has no issue or message dimension.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper measures response to candidate issue positions in a survey conjoint: a hypothetical 2028 presidential race, a national sample of 2024 voters, and partial equilibrium. It does not measure the effect of a canvass contact, and it does not cover the OR-05 or CT-01 House electorates. It shows that a mid-scale partisan score mixes voters who move in opposite directions on any given issue. That implies a midpoint score ranks people by how cross-pressured they are, not by how persuadable they are by an arbitrary message. It does not show that the midpoint is the wrong target overall. The 1-2 pp pooled magnitudes are labeled UNSTRATIFIED and are not a canvass effect size.

bearings.paper_claim: Vote choice responds to a candidate's specific issue positions, and the response depends on where the voter stands on each issue. Effects range from -4.2 pp to +7.3 pp by issue for Republican candidates and from -1.7 pp to +4.5 pp for Democratic candidates. On majority-supported issues, moderating hurts (Republicans -0.0237, SE 0.0048).
bearings.paper_location: pp. 14-19; Figures 3-5; Tables A4, A6, A7
bearings.system_side: Support s is an equal-weight average of direction signals oriented toward the candidate's party. It is built only from party and presidential lean and has no input for the candidate's own positions, so every same-party candidate gets the same s.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper partly supports a party-only baseline: issue effects are modest next to partisanship, and the authors themselves say not to over-read the point estimates. It also shows that a moderate or out-of-step candidate's support is not well proxied by party lean among cross-pressured voters. The evidence comes from the presidential level and a national sample, and candidates were shown without records. Carrying it over to a specific House candidate requires knowing that candidate's issue profile, which Terrier does not hold.

bearings.paper_claim: Public opinion is multidimensional, and voters are often liberal on some issues and conservative on others. Fewer than 10% are consistent across five issues. The authors note an alternative reading: preferences could be one-dimensional with cutlines that differ between voters and elites.
bearings.system_side: Lean is built as 100 x (w_reg x registration + w_vendor x mean(P, O, C)), which assumes that registration and vendor codes lie on one axis. Bands sit at +/-25 and +/-75, and Undetermined is assigned below 0.80 band confidence. Lean is descriptive only and carries no weight in the overall score.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The stakes are low because lean never enters a weighted score. The paper implies that a mid-band or Undetermined lean often marks cross-pressure on issues rather than a centrist or noisy measurement. That reading applies only if the vendor fields embed issue content; registration does not.

bearings.paper_claim: Moving on an issue is rewarded only where the audience disagrees with the current position, and it is penalized where the audience holds that position (Republican candidate, own=R -0.0364 vs own=D +0.0404).
bearings.system_side: PERS is a fixed inverted-U multiplier keyed to each member's stance tier on each topic: Champion 0.10, Highly Persuadable 0.65, Opponent 0.08, and PERS_NONE 0.45 for silence. Because it is applied per topic cell, persuadability is already issue-specific, which matches the paper's issue-level logic.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is an analogy only. The paper studies voters choosing between candidates, not legislators being lobbied. It gives no evidence on legislator persuadability or on the shape of the inverted-U, and it should not be read as calibrating PERS values. Its one structural point, that the target of an appeal is the issue-level disagreement and not the aggregate midpoint, is consistent with PERS being applied per topic.

bearings.paper_claim: Gains and losses across issues and voters can net to modest aggregate effects, so a small average conceals large, opposite-signed issue-level responses. In a stylized case (Figure A7), 50% more voters respond than the net calculation shows.
bearings.system_side: The overall label is a band of the IMP-weighted mean of tier prototypes (Champion 4 ... Opponent -4). A member who is Champion on one topic and Opponent on another can therefore average into a middle band. The F1 money gate and the scenario runner both read this overall label.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is an analogy on how aggregation behaves, with a different population: legislators' issue positions are far more one-dimensional than voters'. The point is a reading caution. A middle overall tier should not be read as 'persuadable everywhere'. Before acting on the overall label, check the dispersion of the per-topic cells. The paper provides no legislator evidence.

gaps_exposed: Terrier has no voter issue-position data. CUA measures consumer exposure to America's Credit Unions (ACU) issues, not policy positions, so it cannot tell a cross-pressured voter from a true centrist. The paper shows that this distinction decides the sign of the response.
Terrier has no input for candidate positions. Support s is identical for every same-party candidate, so the app cannot show how a moderate or out-of-step candidate changes who is persuadable.
The untapped-potential persuasion term has no message or issue dimension. It cannot say which issue to raise with which voter, which is the targeting lever the paper's heterogeneity implies.
The midpoint-peaked persuasion term (1 - |2s - 1|) has never been validated against observed persuasion heterogeneity, whether from a canvass RCT or a survey.
Melange's overall stance tier does not surface how spread out a member's per-topic tiers are, so a mixed Champion/Opponent record looks the same as a uniformly neutral one.
flags: Out-of-population citation: Paul's component positions list Broockman & Kalla 2026 under melange-influence-engine.persuadability-table. The paper measures voters' response to candidate positions, not whether legislators can be persuaded by lobbying. It cannot calibrate PERS or support the inverted-U, and the bearing is analogy only.

Annotation conflation: Paul's position for terrier-canvass.untapped-potential describes heavily highlighted door-canvass protocol material (nonjudgmental exchange, perspective-getting, a 7-minute version). That material comes from Kalla & Broockman 2020, not this 2026 paper. This paper has no canvass protocol.

The pooled AMCEs (Democrats +1.1 pp, Republicans +1.8 pp; N = 180,000 respondent x task x candidate x policy rows per party, from 6,000 respondents) span a known fault line: majority versus non-majority issues, and the respondent's own position. Quote them only with those strata, or label them UNSTRATIFIED.
Paul's annotation files for this work hold only bibliography entries. The 40 PDF highlights carry no note text, so none of his takeaways can be confirmed.
The venue and DOI (10.31235/osf.io/bvjtd_v1) are unverified from the PDF text. The manuscript is dated March 11, 2026.
Any application of these findings to Terrier or Melange is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
No conflict with D-021, D-025, or the two rejected SNA proposals: the paper argues for none of them.
rel.paul_alignment: The evidence agrees with the gist of Paul's highlights: returns to moderation are issue-specific, backfire on majority-held positions, and add up to modest averages even though voters care about issues. It agrees with his one recorded component note on terrier-canvass.candidate-support ('returns to moderation are issue-specific'). That note is now stale against the built system. Terrier's support score and its untapped-potential persuasion term, live since 2026-10-09, are purely one-dimensional partisan composites with no issue input, so the insight he highlighted is not encoded anywhere. His listing of the paper under the Melange persuadability table goes beyond the paper's evidence, which concerns voters, not legislators. The canvass-protocol material he attributes alongside it belongs to Kalla & Broockman 2020.

related.why: Same authors. That paper supplies the door-canvass persuasion protocol, which Paul's untapped-potential notes attribute alongside this paper. This paper supplies the issue-position heterogeneity that a canvass would need to target.
It quantifies returns to tailoring messages to voter subgroups, which is the operational answer to this paper's finding that persuasion response differs by issue and by voter position.
It tests microtargeted, issue-tailored persuasion. This paper explains why tailoring by issue should matter: cross-pressured voters respond with opposite signs on different issues.

NOMINATE gives the one-dimensional account of elite (roll-call) ideology. This paper finds mass opinion is multidimensional relative to that elite axis, which is why elite-middle moves do not map onto the median voter.

CFscores place donors and candidates on one ideological dimension. This paper's cross-pressure finding cautions against reading a voter's or candidate's single-axis position as their position on any particular issue.
An agent-based model of micro-targeted campaigning. Issue-specific, voter-position-dependent persuasion of the kind measured here is the empirical input such a model would need.
